title: Fatimah's hands
hookLine: her hands are rough from the mill, and she's given the tasbih instead of a servant (Bukhari)

lines: THE PROPHET'S DAUGHTER AT THE MILL.
cards: Two flat stones, one on top of the other, with a wooden handle set in the top one. You pour grain in the hole and turn, and turn, and flour creeps out the edge.
That's a hand mill, and in Medina someone had to turn one every day, or there was no bread. In the house of Ali and Fatimah, that someone was Fatimah.
The Prophet's daughter, the one he called a part of him, had hands that showed it. Today: Fatimah's hands, and what her father gave her for them.

teach.b: Ali describes her work in a report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. She turned the mill until it marked her hand. She carried water in a skin until the strap marked her.
She swept the house until her clothes were dusty, and kept the fire under the pot.
When captives came to Medina, Ali suggested she ask her father for a servant. Bukhari tells what came next. She went, he wasn't home, and she left word.
That night he came to their house, sat down between them, and taught them words for bedtime: Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhanallah thirty-three, alhamdulillah thirty-three.
And he said: this is better for you than a servant. We met those words on an earlier day. Today, look at the hands.

He didn't tell her the work was beneath her. He didn't take it away, either. Aisha, asked what the Prophet did at home, says in Bukhari that he served his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray.
Work first, in the house, with his own hands; then prayer. So what did Fatimah receive? Not a way out of the mill.

teach.h: BETTER FOR YOU THAN A SERVANT.
teach.b: The words come at the end of the day, when the hands are finally still. Ali said in a report in Bukhari that he never left them off after that night.
Some readers see here a household that lived on little, where tiredness itself was met with remembrance. The hands stayed rough. The night got words.

how: Muslims say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar before sleep, following this hadith, and the set is often called the tasbih of Fatimah.

o: her careful handwriting of the Qur'an's first verses
her hands, rough from the mill, the water and the broom
her gift for healing the sick with a single touch

s: the Prophet told Fatimah the housework was beneath her
he didn't take the work away; he gave words to carry it.
the Prophet helped with work at home
Aisha says in Bukhari that he served his family, then went out to pray.
Ali said he kept saying the words after that night
in Bukhari, Ali says he never left them off.

games.q: you're Fatimah. your hands are marked from the mill, and captives have come to Medina. Ali suggests you ask your father for a servant. what happens?
o: you get a servant the next day.
your father comes at night and gives you words instead.
your father says the work is not for you.
games.why: he came that night, sat between them, and taught the words for bedtime: better for you than a servant.

practice: This week ran from Zaynab, mother of the poor, through Juwayriyyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Maria, to Fatimah.
Think back over what your hands did today, dishes, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a child's coat, and let each task come and go before you rest them.
If you pray, say subhanallah, alhamdulillah, Allahu akbar, slowly; if not, just feel tired hands go still.

wordCard.voice: Fatimah's hands. Rough from the mill, and given words for the end of the day instead of a servant. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: glorifying God, saying subhanallah; the bedtime set is often called the tasbih of Fatimah.

carryVoice: Your line: better than a servant. Rough hands, and words to end the day. That's day eight hundred nineteen.
